note: Extended south from Eglinton to Bloor in 1796 by William Berczy.
Queen's Rangers started at Eglinton in 1795 and worked north, reaching Holland Landing (St. Albans) on 16 February 1796.
No year sourced. Too swampy for a main road at first; a path called the 'road to Yonge Street' existed; southern end in use in the first decade of the 19th century.
Route extended from Queen Street to the harbour in 1812; gravelled 1828.
Opened 8 August 1958. (South Kingsway stands in for the Humber, the edge of the map.)
Opened 1 August 1962.
Westbound lanes from York Street opened 3 December 1962; eastbound Spadina to York opened 1963.
Completed 1964; opened 6 November 1964 together with the Parkway south of Bloor (date from the Don Valley Parkway article).
'Gardiner East', opened July 1966. DEMOLISHED: Don River to Leslie Street taken down in 2001; remaining stub east of the Parkway ramps demolished October 2021.
First section, opened 31 August 1961 (Eglinton is outside the old city). Applied to the whole parkway; the Gardiner to Bloor row below replaces it there.
Third section, opened 6 November 1964; built over existing roadways. (Eastern Avenue and the viaduct stand in for the Gardiner and Bloor.)

Built on Toronto Harbour Commission fill (waterfront project started 1914; Sunnyside section filled in the 1910s-early 1920s). Route pushed east to Bathurst Street on 28 January 1924, taking in Laburnam Avenue, Starr Avenue and Dominion Street. Widened to six lanes in the 1950s with the Gardiner; the stretch south of Exhibition Place sits on 1950s fill. (Windermere Avenue stands in for the Humber.)

Formerly Fleet Street (and Harbour Street connections), older streets joined in the 1950s as the Gardiner service road; renamed Lake Shore Boulevard 25 August 1959. 1959 is the renaming, not the first opening of the roadway. Year left blank: 1959 is a renaming of older streets.

Formerly Keating Street (Cherry to Leslie) plus a new extension to Woodbine Avenue (construction began 1955 per the Gardiner article); renamed Lake Shore Boulevard 25 August 1959. Year left blank: 1959 is a renaming of older streets.
No exact year sourced. Created on reclaimed land in the inner harbour; harbour filled 'sometime after 1919 to the early 1920s'.
Opened 1829 as College Avenue, a private entrance to King's College, cut 120 feet wide.
Ended at Queen Street until 1931, when it was extended south to Front Street.
Opened 1829 as the other private entrance to King's College (also called College Avenue).
Built by Dr. William Baldwin beginning in 1815; name first on published maps 1834.
Southern portion was Brock Street, 'first appearing around 1837'; kept that name until after 1884.
No opening year sourced. Surveyed as the first concession road north of Lot (Queen) Street; tollgate at Yonge 1820; called Sydenham Road 1844-1854; named Bloor by 1855.
Prince Edward Viaduct. Carries Bloor Street over the Don valley; completed 1918 (the Rosedale Valley Bridge article says the viaduct opened in 1918). Cross streets not stated in the source.

Laid out as Lot Street in Aitkin's original 1793 survey, the baseline for the park lots; renamed Queen Street 1844. Applied from Dufferin to River Street: the stretch drawn as a road on the Chewett map of 1834.
Laid out and named in the original 1793 plan of York (original stretch = the ten-block townsite; later extensions not dated in the source).
Original Dundas Street ran from Queen and Ossington north on Ossington, then west; extended east to York by Asa Danforth in 1797. Applies to Dundas west of Ossington.
Formerly Arthur Street, connected 'in the latter half of the 19th century' (no year).
Formerly St. Patrick Street (Anderson Street east of McCaul); cut through the Grange estate in 1877.
Formerly Agnes Street (no opening year sourced); became part of Dundas by the 1920s.
Jog between Agnes Street and Wilton Street eliminated 1922-1923 (formerly Crookshank Street).
Formerly Wilton Street / Wilton Crescent / Beech Street (no opening year sourced).
Steel arch bridge over the Don built 1910-1911.
Ended at Broadview from the 1920s to the 1940s; extended east to Kingston Road 'in the 1950s' (no year).

Originally New Street (later Nelson), 'the first new north-south street in the first expansion of York'. The 1797 date of that expansion comes from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York,_Upper_Canada, not from the Jarvis Street article.

Samuel Jarvis began selling the family property in 1846; his house Hazel Burn was demolished to make way for Jarvis Street. 1846 = start of the subdivision, not a stated opening date. (Charles Street stands in for Bloor, where the street file ends Jarvis.)
Clifton Road Extension through Rosedale, approved 1946/1949, renamed Mount Pleasant Road 23 January 1950 and opened to traffic 17 May (1950).
New road through Mount Pleasant Cemetery (by-law 1915), opened 1919 from St. Clair to the Blythwood ravine; bridge and extension to Lawrence 1934-1936.
No opening year sourced. Council approved expropriating a 66-foot roadway through the ravine in 1887 (by-law registered 1888); grading and construction 'in the 1890s'.
Bayview Extension, built with the Don Valley Parkway project; extended south from Moore Avenue to Front Street in 1959. Applied to all of Bayview inside the old city, which is the extension.
Originally Bear Street; renamed Bay Street in 1797, linking Lot (Queen) Street to the bay.
Terauley Street until 1922, when it became part of Bay Street (the street itself is older; opening year not sourced). Year left blank: 1922 is a renaming.
By-Law 9316 (1922) joined St. Vincent, Chapel and North streets and filled the gaps.
By-Law 9884, 28 January 1924: Ketchum Avenue renamed Bay Street.
No year sourced. Laid out 'in the late 18th century' as the Third Concession road; first settlement at Yonge 1837.
Built 1851 by the Don and Danforth Plank Road Company from Broadview (Don Mills Road) east.
Asa Danforth's road, contracted 1799, completed 18 December 1800; resurveyed 1815 and rebuilt as the Kingston Road by 1817.
Indigenous trail far older than the town; 'by 1797 it was known as Davenport Road'. 1797 is the first documented name, not a construction date.
Constructed 1798 by Timothy Skinner as the Mill Road / Don Mills Road; renamed Broadview 1884.
Bridge over the Don opened 16 December 1923. Cross streets are my reading of the bridge location, not stated in the source.
Realigned east of Yonge in 1930 to meet College Street. Year left blank: a realignment, not an opening.
